newsitem.title: CANADA: FORECAST-Canada poised for economic gains in 1997. [CORRECTED 19:15 GMT]
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Canada poised for economic gains in 1997. [CORRECTED 19:15 GMT]

text.p: Hopes for a sustained economic recovery in Canada will prove well-placed in 1997 as the country racks up impressive industrial growth and healthy trade balances, a Reuters poll of economists showed.

The quarterly Reuters survey, which polled twenty-two economists in Canada and the United States, reveals a growing belief that Canada's economy will emerge as one of the top performers among the G7 nations this year.
Twenty economists in the survey predicted that, on average, quarter-on-quarter gross domestic product (GDP) growth will climb to a highwater mark of 3.7 percent by the second quarter of 1997.
Canada's GDP currently sits at 3.3 percent for the third quarter of 1996.
Growth will remain above three percent throughout 1997 before slipping to 2.6 percent in the third quarter of 1998, the economists forecast.

A combination of low interest rates, a lower-than-expected federal budget deficit and improved consumer confidence provide the bounce to this economic rebound, said John Anania, an economist with the Royal Bank of Canada.
"This growth is totally investment-led with some pick-up on the consumer side in 1997," Anania said. "Interest rates should stay pretty flat, and that means continued above-trend growth."

The Bank of Canada has cut its key bank rate by a total of 500 basis points since May 1995. The bank rate, currently 3.25 percent, is the top of the central bank's target range for overnight lending to financial institutions.
The bank rate determines prime lending rates by the commercial banks, which are currently at 4.75 percent -- the lowest level since 1959.
Although Anania does not anticipate a major shift in interest rates, he foresees some monetary tightening on the currency side.
The Canadian dollar is currently worth US$0.7448.
Twenty of the survey's economists predicted the Canadian currency will appreciate to US$0.77 by the fourth quarter of 1998.
If the Canadian dollar rises past US$0.76, the Bank of Canada will start intervening more regularly, Anania said.
A stronger dollar also poses a threat to Canada's blossoming merchandise trade surplus, which is expected to widen to C$7.0 billion (US$5.2 billion) in the fourth quarter of 1996.
Canada's trade surplus stands at C$5.4 billion (US$4.0 billion) for the third quarter of 1996.
Survey participants predicted even further trade growth with the average quarterly surplus rising to C$10.1 billion (US$7.5 billion) by the third quarter of 1998.
Expanding Canada's international trade -- especially in Asia -- has been one of Prime Minister Jean Chretien's main preoccupations in office.
Last week, Chretien returned from a 12-day trade mission to South Korea, the Philippines and Thailand, brandishing more than C$2.0 billion (US$1.5 billion) in trade deals.
While not dismissing the economic impact of such trips, economists cite economic growth in the United States -- Canada's largest trading partner -- for the trade parade.
The comparatively higher U.S. inflation and interest rates will generate a good surplus in the trade balance this year - a trend that will slow in 1998 as exports to Canada increase, Anania said.
U.S. inflation, as measured in the core consumer price index (CPI), is running at 3.3 percent year-on-year.
Canada's annual inflation rate -- the CPI excluding food and energy -- ran at 1.6 percent for the third quarter of 1996.
Statistics Canada's announcement last week that the CPI had jumped for the third month in a row elicited a collective shrug from market watchers.

"Despite a 2.6-percent rise over the last three-month period, inflation is certainly not staging a comback," said Michel Doucet, an economist with Montreal-based brokerage Levesque Beaubien Geoffrion.
Doucet said there remains some slack in the Canadian economy because productive capacity grew faster than aggregate demand in the first half of the year.
Canada's output gap, the amount by which an economy can grow without triggering inflation, is estimated at 3.0 to 3.5 percent.
The one dark cloud in an otherwise bright economic picture is reserved for unemployed Canadians.
Strong growth and increased trade opportunities will only shave a thin layer off Canada's stubbornly high jobless numbers, the economists predicted.
Although all those surveyed agreed unemployment would gradually decline during the next two years, only one of the 22 economists polled predicted a jobless rate under 9.0 percent this year.
Canada's unemployment rate in December (corrects from November) 1996 was 9.7 percent.
((Reuters Toronto Bureau (416) 941-8100))
